LOCKDOWN CRIMINAL RECORDS

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

Unique Selling Point:
More than 100,000 South Africans were arrested within the first 21-days of our country's lockdown. After paying admission guilt fines or bail, many of them now face additional hardships because of the criminal record they have attached to their names. When will their records be expunged? In the meantime how is their lives affected?


Summary:
In January, Police Minister Nathi Mthetwa announced that more than 20 000 people have been arrested for violating the lockdown regulations. Close to 8 000 of them were nabbed for not wearing a mask in public. No matter how “minor” these offenses are, criminal records have been recorded against those who had such encounters with the police. With the country still fighting Coronavirus, many are worried that the government will not expunge the criminal records of those who violated the lockdown regulations. For this story, we will speak to people who were arrested and are already being affected by the consequences of living with a criminal record. They say they are being prevented from gaining employment, acquiring a travel visa to other countries and more. According to data, the majority of convicted cases related to the failure to confine to residence during the lockdown period.

Further information:
The South African Police Service may give a person, who has been arrested on suspicion of a less serious crime, an option to pay an admission of guilt fine.

Such a fine allows a person to admit guilt for a less serious offence without having to appear in court. This prevents an unnecessary overload of the court system.

It is meant to resolve less serious matters quickly, where an accused person accepts responsibility for having committed a minor offence. However, people who pay an admission of guilt also attract a criminal record.

The South African Judiciary has published a series of directives which outline how much citizens will have to pay in ‘admission of guilt’ fines if they are found to breach the country’s lockdown rules.

The directives are based on provincial and magistrate districts, and are in line with the new level 4 lockdown regulations which were introduced from 1 May.

The directives also provide on how the court plans to deal with these cases, with KZN indicating that it will reserve judgement for breaches it deems trivial.

Press Release:


Lockdown Record for Life?
Last year Carte Blanche reported on allegations of unwarranted brutality and violence when police arrested people for breaking COVID-19 lockdown regulations. Now, we revisit the dilemma of at least 200,000 South Africans arrested for offences like not wearing masks and allegedly breaking curfew. Many spent time behind bars or paid hefty fines of up to R5000. Many still were let go with the option of signing an admission of guilt – something which didn’t sound terrible at the time and helped them not spend time in police custody. But in the long run, it’s saddled them with criminal records that are hampering life as they knew it – with no indication from the government on whether these might be expunged after the pandemic.
Producer: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje | Presenter: Bongani Bingwa

Script:


SCRIPT - LOCKDOWN CRIMINAL RECORDS
PRESENTER - BONGANI BINGWA
PRODUCER - BUSISIWE GUMEDE-CHIZHANJE

VO - In March last year, the government introduced the Disaster Management Act
which regulates curfew, gathering in groups and not wearing masks in public
spaces.
UPSOUND - Go home, where are you going?
- I’m going back home
Since then over 400 000 South Africans have spent time behind bars or paid hefty
fines of between R500- R5000 for failing to adhere to the regulations.
Bongani Link - Within two months of the imposition of lockdown more than 200 000
south africans were arrested for contravening the lockdown rules Many of those were let
go with the option of an admission of guilt. It's a fine that doesn't sound so serious but
it's a stain that will stay with a lot of them for a very long time.
VO - An admission of guilt fine allows people who are accused of committing a
minor offense, to take responsibility without having to appear in court. Defense
Lawyer William Booth says it’s a tempting offer, but one which has earned many
of those arrested during lockdown criminal records.
SOUND UP (William Booth) 8:15 - often people don’t know how it affects them in the
future
VO - Thabo Malatji says he wasn't aware of this, when he had a brush with the law
in April 2020. He was arrested for not wearing a mask in public when he was
walking home from buying essentials at Phumulani Mall in Tembisa.
SOUND UP ( Thabiso Malatji) - I came out of the mall and was walking home.. I saw the
police and SANDF approaching me. They asked, “where is your mask?”. They say “you
don't have a mask, let’s go”. They put me in the police van with my groceries. 15:51-

VO – MALATJI spent the night in jail and was released on bail the following day.
He was eager to move on from the traumatic experience, but UNBEKNOWN to

him, his problems were just getting started. He works as a delivery driver which
requires a Professional Driver’s Permit. Months after his arrest he discovered that
he cannot renew his PERMIT as he now has a criminal record.
SOUND UP (Thabo Malaji) 12:23- So if I can’t renew my license by August, I’m going
to lose my job. The company I work for has a rule that I can’t drive for them without my
PDP licence.
VO - Malatji fears that he will lose his job…and he still struggles with the memory
of his first night in a holding cell.
Bongani Link - the whole point of restrictions is to limit the spread of the disease,
so we have masks and you don't want people in crowded and closed spaces.
What do you do when they don't obey? You put them behind bars in enclosed
and crowded spaces.
VO - Malatji feared contracting COVID-19 in the communal holding cell that he
was sharing with several other detainees.
SOUND UP - Thabo Malatji - 17:58 It was full. 18:12- The entire time we were in there
they didn’t even give us our masks.
VO - This was also Dr Hinner Koster’s concern on the 13th of February, when he,
together with his partner Ensli Strydom and their friend Seugnet Te Groen, spent
a night at the Silverlakes Police Station.
SOUND UP - 14:52 – 15:03There was no social distancing, no sanitising stuff, if they
wanna catch you for curfew at least have things in place at the cells as well.
VO - Koster was nabbed outside of his estate, for missing curfew, by what he
says, were a few minutes. All three of them were driving back from a function
when they realised a police van was following them.

SOUND UP - Dr Kostler - 04:56 – 05:06 And then we stopped at the gate...aAnd then
they jumped out and then they started having quite an 05:07 – 05:19 Aggressive
attitude towards us...they just started immediately saying that Sonnet was doing
reckless driving, she was chasing 05:20 – 05:32 Away from them and then we said but
it’s not true, all we wanted to do was go to a safer place to ensure that we are safe.
VO - VO - After a heated exchange the police allegedly demanded that the three
follow them to the police station, where the women say they were physically
abused.

SOUND UP - SONNET - 05:38 They tried to put me into the cell. As they took me to
the cell i told them im claustrophobic please, let me just be with Ensly, I don’t want to go
alone in this cell. The next moment I had a steel thing in my eye, that was the
pepperspray, also my tooth was chipped because they pushed the pepper spray into my
mouth.
Bongani 06:18 so as they put you in the cell they ppersprayed you?
Sonnet: Yes
Bongani: For what reason?

Sonnet: To teach us a lesson. They also did the same with Ensli.
SOUND UP - Ensli - 08:38 She came into the cells and said im going to teach you a
lesson. And she sprayed pepper spray in my eyes.
VO - Similar cases of alleged police brutality were under the spotlight during hard
lockdown. We covered a spike in reports of intimidation and violence against
citizens in May 2020. A year on, and many of those who had run-ins with the
police are saddled with criminal records.
VO - The three friends were released the next day after being charged for
breaching the curfew and resisting arrest. Their case was thrown out of court four
days later.

20:20 – 20:34 They just looked at it before hand and they said this is not worth the
case to waste time on
BONGANI 20:40 – 20:41 You don’t want to let this go do you?
20:42 – 20:50 No we don’t, I think if people like ourselves don’t come to the front
this will just keep on continuing.20:54 – 21:01We heard about all the other cases.
21:02 – 21:14 People don’t want to actually want to..think from an emotional side
or the financial side they. Its difficult for them to take the case further against the police.
VO - Another man that is living in Limbo is John Mabutsela from Alexandra
township. He was arrested in April 2020 at a wedding celebration, a few hours
after curfew went into effect.
02:25 The night I was arrested it was on level 5 lockdown. My brother was getting
married.

04:23 Bongani: Why didn’t you go home when the time was up?
John: Honestly to you, we were having a good time, We wanted to go home. The
groomsman didn't want us to go. He said guys please don't go. It's my day.
BONGANI LINK _ It’s practically mission impossible, alexandra township is one of
the most densely populated areas in south africa, enforcing lockdown restrictions
was always going to be a challenge at the best of times.
VO - Mabitsela also spent a night in jail and was released the following morning.
He was able to get legal assistance, but his lawyer advised to pay a fine…and
NOW he says he’s stuck with a criminal record that’s affecting his prospects of
finding a new job after being retrenched in the economic turmoil caused by the
pandemic.
SOUND UP (John) 24:15 I was almost changing my life, to get a job. They said I’ve got
a criminal record. What must I do now with that? So I can not be employed anymore”
SOUND UP (Bongani ; John but some people will say you broke the law?
SOUND UP (John) 26:21 I will show my remorse that i have broken the law. I’ll never do
it again. So can i just clear my name on that one
VO - Booth recommends that people arrested for contravening the lockdown
regulations shouldn’t sign the admission of guilt form as it could take years for
their records to be expunged.
SOUND UP ( William Booth) 10:13- Go see a lawyer and then they can approach the
prosecutors to try and have the charges withdrawn, then no criminal record.
VO - The Department of Justice says it is aware that some cases related to the
COVID-19 lockdown will attract criminal records if fines are paid.
Minister of Justice spokesperson Chrispin Phiri says the department has been
working to raise awareness about its long-term implications.

SOUND UP (Bongani Bingwa)15:06 – 15:17 Do you accept that most people who
are told to sign an admission of guilt may do so without knowing that they could
potentially have a criminal record for up to 10 years?

15:18 – 15:27 (Chrispin Phiri) I think the department of justice through our office of the
deputy minister has actually gone out quite strongly to inform people that, be
knowledgeable about this signing an admission of guilt is ultimately getting yourself a
criminal record..
VO - Admission of guilt fines have long been on the government’s raider, outside of
lockdown. But the issue can only be addressed through an amendment in the
Judicial Matters Bill.
SOUND UP (Chrispian Phiri)07:49 – 07:55 We had already looked at draft
legislation to deal with these types of problems, as you know passing a bill is subject to
parliament also deliberating on it and really taking the executive honour what the type of
thinking was
BONGANI 8:40 – 08:53 But as things stand, if you have a criminal record from a
contravention of lockdown regulations for example, that’s a record that could
stand for all those years?
(CHRISPIN OHIRI) 08:54 – 08:58 That is the law as we speak today.
VO - Phiri says expunging criminal records incurred during lockdown is not a
priority right now, especially with a third COVID-19 wave looming.
12:16 – 12:23 (Bongani Bingwa) It just seems like we’re using a sledge
hammer to kill a fly..
12:24 – 12:34 Well it’s definitely not a fly we're killing here. 12These regulations
are not there arbitrarily,like what we are seeing in India is quite sad though.
VO - Booth says the lockdown regulations stipulate that law enforcement officers
should warn a person who violated regulations before arresting them. This man,

Naas Le Roux says no officer bothered to give him a warning before he was
arrested.

VO - This video from the night shows Le Roux trying to explain to officers that
he broke the curfew to buy formula for his new born baby,
SOUND UP - Le Roux Video UPSOUND. Are you arresting me? He doesn't want to
identify himself here.
SOUND UP (Le Roux) We realised natasha breast milk is starting to dry up..2:55 we
decided we have to find a substitute thats formula milk.
VO - VO – Le Roux and Koster believe the police didn’t want to reason with them
because they had a point to prove. MALATJI on the other hand believes the
police had a target to reach.
SOUND UP Thabo- 16:18- ...One of the police officers asked how many we were in
there and the one by the door said 8. The officers mentioned that their target was 10
people. 16:39- Then along the way they arrested two more people to reach this target.
They then took us all to the police station.
VO - Le Roux and Koster were able to get their charges withdrawn because they
had the access to legal aid.
SOUND UP - Koster
21:30 – 21:39Those that were there that evening. They must get out of the police
force. I want to feel safe if I approach a policeman.
But people like Malatji, who aren't as financially stable, now face living with
criminal records – with the limitations that it imposes.
SOUND UP - (thabo)
18:55 ...I would rather be told that I am going to prison or not than to be strung along
for this long not knowing if I can continue with my life because now everything says I’m
a criminal. 19:32- And if I’m a criminal, they must lock me up and I’ll do my time.

metadata.Unique Selling Point: More than 100,000 South Africans were arrested within the first 21-days of our country's lockdown. After paying admission guilt fines or bail, many of them now face additional hardships because of the criminal record they have attached to their names. When will their records be expunged? In the meantime how is their lives affected?
metadata.Summary: In January, Police Minister Nathi Mthetwa announced that more than 20 000 people have been arrested for violating the lockdown regulations. Close to 8 000 of them were nabbed for not wearing a mask in public. No matter how “minor” these offenses are, criminal records have been recorded against those who had such encounters with the police. With the country still fighting Coronavirus, many are worried that the government will not expunge the criminal records of those who violated the lockdown regulations. For this story, we will speak to people who were arrested and are already being affected by the consequences of living with a criminal record. They say they are being prevented from gaining employment, acquiring a travel visa to other countries and more. According to data, the majority of convicted cases related to the failure to confine to residence during the lockdown period.
metadata.Further information: The South African Police Service may give a person, who has been arrested on suspicion of a less serious crime, an option to pay an admission of guilt fine. Such a fine allows a person to admit guilt for a less serious offence without having to appear in court. This prevents an unnecessary overload of the court system. It is meant to resolve less serious matters quickly, where an accused person accepts responsibility for having committed a minor offence. However, people who pay an admission of guilt also attract a criminal record. The South African Judiciary has published a series of directives which outline how much citizens will have to pay in ‘admission of guilt’ fines if they are found to breach the country’s lockdown rules. The directives are based on provincial and magistrate districts, and are in line with the new level 4 lockdown regulations which were introduced from 1 May. The directives also provide on how the court plans to deal with these cases, with KZN indicating that it will reserve judgement for breaches it deems trivial.
